newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - March 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - March 4.

text.p: Senior Coalition partner National on Monday rushed to paper over the latest cracks in its accord with NZ First, with Health Minister Bill English saying plans for a private consortium to run a Christchurch Hospital cardiac unit may "fall over" anyway. Associate Health Minister Neil Kirton, a NZ First MP, has argued that the proposed joint venture between Healthcare Otago and the privately owned Southern Cardiothoracic Institute contradicts the spirit of the Coalition accord that allows for only "limited" involvement by private companies in public hospital services. Page 1.

Government MPs will discuss today the trial use of covert speed cameras, despite a promise at their introduction in 1993 that the cameras would not be hidden. The Cabinet has already approved the proposal but it is expected to be discussed at NZ First and National caucus meetings today, with the announcement of a go-ahead possible later this week. Page 2.

National list MP Katherine O'Regan is investigating speculation that the party will stay out of the Tauranga electorate of NZ First leader Winston Peters at the next election to avoid a campaign battle with its Coalition partner. Talk within party ranks has suggested the move could be part of the Coalition deal, though O'Regan and electorate chairwoman Barbara Steele said on Monday that they were unaware of any formal discussion. Page 2.

The Alliance looks set to get nowhere with its bid for a second seat on Parliament's Maori affairs select committee. A spokeswoman for the Leader of the House, Wyatt Creech, said on Monday that increasing the number of committee members to accommodate Alliance list MP Alamein Kopu would go against Parliament's Standing Orders, the rules that govern proceedings in the House. Page 2.

The public will receive an indication today of where the government's spending priorities will lie in the next financial year when Treasurer Winston Peters delivers his first budget policy statement. The statement, required by the Fiscal Responsibility Act, will provide details of the government's overall spending plans, its expected tax take and overall financial position in the next few years. Page 2.

Auckland casino operator Sky City made an after-tax profit of $18.2 million for the six months to December, and is on track to meet its full-year forecast profit of $35.8 million. But the company was hit by unspecified losses at its new theatre and lower-than-expected returns from its food and drink and carparking operations. Sky's shares closed at $7.00, down 20 cents. Page 13.

Fertiliser and chemical company Fernz Corporation is confident of achieving its forecast annual profit, earning two-thirds of the total profit in the second half of the year. Fernz reported an unaudited tax-paid profit of $16.1 million for the six months to November 30, a 3.4 percent rise on the matching period the previous year. Page 13.

A price war has broken out between rival video games console manufacturers Sony PlayStation and Sega Saturn with both dropping the price of their units by up to $100. Sony Computer Entertainment New Zealand fired the opening shot on Friday, lowering the price of its PlayStation machines to $299.95 from $399.95. Sega Saturn followed to match that price on Monday, taking $80 of its system. Page 13.

Some retailers are likely to face relatively tough trading conditions for the rest of 1997, according to the ANZ Bank. Retail sales growth in the next six months will be "modest at best" and will probably fall for discretionary goods, ANZ Bank says in Retailers Focus. The report was done for the Retail and Wholesale Merchants Association. Page 13.

The budget policy statement today is expected to show that the government has back-tracked on its new spending intentions for the coming year -- from the promised $1.2 billion to less than $1 billion. The New Zealand Herald understands that it has simply not been possible to get many of the initiatives to the stage where they can be included in this year's budget, which will be delivered in June. Just where the knife of the Treasurer, Winston Peters, will be used to pare back government spending is not yet clear.

The more experienced and wily gamblers have caused the operator of the Auckland casino to work harder for its profit. In reporting a $18.2 million tax-paid profit for the six months to December 31, the casino operator, Sky City Ltd, said its average take each day from a table was $2,800, down from $3,200 in the five months to June 30. The managing director, Evan Davies, said the figure of $2,800 was significantly ahead of the $2,340 forecast in the company's listing profile last year.

Power New Zealand has lost its legal battle to have Mercury Energy's takeover bid ruled anti-competitive. The Court of Appeal on Monday, upheld, like the High Court before it, the Commerce Commission's decision in late 1994 to clear Mercury to take over its northern neighbour.

Some retailers are likely to face relatively tough trading conditions over the remainder of 1997, the ANZ Bank says. "Talking to retailers, we believe the weakness in retailing evident during the Christmas period has continued in the first two months of 1997," ANZ's chief economist, Paul Stewart, said.

Telecom's Xtra service is in the firing line again with complaints to the Commerce Commission and action in the Auckland High Court by internet service providers. Ron Woodrow, the chairman of the Internet Service Providers Association of New Zealand (Ispanz), which comprises most of the country's providers except for Clear Communications and Telecom, said his group has prepared a complaint dealing with Telecom's alleged predatory pricing of its Xtra Internet Service.

Full employment -- defined as an unemployment rate of one to two percent -- is achievable by the year 2000 if the Employment Contracts Acts is retained, says the Business Roundtable executive director, Roger Kerr. "I suspect most people still do not take that proposition seriously," Kerr told an Institute for International Research Conference on industrial relations in Auckland on Monday.

The developer of Auckland's Britomart complex, Pacific Capital Assets, confirmed its intention to seek a sharemarket listing on Monday. Details of the timing and size of the float have yet to be announced. However, it is believed that the public issue will be between $60 million and $70 million, of which a portion will be taken up by existing shareholders.

The New Zealand dollar ended more than half a cent above Friday's finish at US$0.6958 on Monday, despite some late afternoon selling from Asia which knocked it off its early peak of 0.6978. The kiwi added to gains made in New York in early local trading as speculators scrambled to buy it to cover short positions established in Friday's sell-off.
